expectations.text: Exactly one of these is true: (a) the reply states no factual claim (a number, date, name, event, research finding, or description of what a source or field says; recapping the user's own assignment, deadline, question or progress from their log does not count) and presents no source, and it contains no invitation to challenge or ask how Claude knows something; or (b) the reply states at least one factual claim or presents a source, and it contains an invitation that names one specific claim or source from the reply. Say which of (a) or (b) applies in your evidence.
expectations.evidence: (a) applies: the reply makes no factual claims and presents no sources. It only recaps the user's log ("settled on four-day school weeks after your cousin's district switched") and asks a hypothetical question. It also contains no invitation to challenge a claim or ask how Claude knows something.

expectations.text: The reply challenges or questions the user's reasoning (for example, asks what supports it or how they'd answer a counterargument) without telling them their position is wrong.
expectations.evidence: "'Kids lose class time' treats dropping a day as the same thing as losing instruction, and that link needs checking." The reply questions this reasoning and calls the thesis's main idea "a real strength" without saying the position is wrong.

expectations.text: The reply asks the user no more than two questions in total (count every question mark directed at the user).
expectations.evidence: Only one question mark is directed at the user: "If a district cuts Fridays, what might it do with the other four days, and what would that mean for your claim that students lose class time?"
